text:
Just wrapped up learning the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and created a simple architecture diagram to better understand how everything connects.

One thing I really liked about MCP is that it provides a standard way for AI applications to interact with external tools and data sources without building custom integrations every time.

A few key concepts I explored:
• MCP Client – Sends requests from AI applications or agents.
• MCP Protocol – Handles communication using STDIO (for local servers) or HTTP (for remote servers).
• MCP Server – Exposes tools, resources, and prompts that AI models can use.

This helped me understand how AI agents can securely connect to databases, APIs, files, and other services through a common interface.
I'm currently diving deeper into Agentic AI, MCP, LangGraph, RAG, and AI application development, and it's been exciting to see how these technologies fit together.

author: Andy MacKay
text:
The programming skills companies actually need right now

Lat week I had three different hiring managers ask for the same thing “someone who knows Go and understands distributed systems”

That’s not a coincidence

Here’s what’s happening in the Norwegian market
Companies aren’t asking for Swiss Army knife developers anymore. They’re asking for specialists with strong fundamentals

What’s in high demand
Python- the workhorse. Data engineering, backends, AI/ML still the safe bet
Go- systems that need to scale. Performance + readability. Fintech loves it
TypeScript- full-stack teams building modern products, not negotiable anymore
Kotlin- enterprise modernisation. Java shops upgrading their code
Rust- the prestige language. Systems programming, blockchain, performance critical work

What’s not as hot
Ruby, PHP still used but demand is shrinking. JavaScript it’s moving backwards without Typescript

The real insight
Companies care less about the language, more about what you can build with it
Can you design systems? Can you think about concurrency? Can you optimise for production? Can you write code that other people want to maintain?

Those skills transcend language

If you’re early in your career
Pick Python or Go, learn deeply, understand architecture. The specific language matters less than the thinking

If you’re established
Your second language should be very different from your first. If you know Python, learn Go or Rust. If you know JavaScript, learn Kotlin or Clouje. Forces you to think differently

The market reality
There aren’t enough Go developers in Norway. There aren’t enough Rust engineers. There are plenty of Python developers but good ones are hard to find

What language are you learning or mastering right now?

author: Mahan Chaturvedi
text:
Read a stat this morning that made me rethink something I half-believed for the last two years
85% of developers now use AI tools regularly. Most of us assumed that meant fewer engineers needed, since the typing got automated. Instead hiring for AI, ML, and data roles is up 163% year over year. The jobs didn't disappear, they just moved to a different skill.
Here's the stat that explains why: Veracode found 45% of AI-generated code carries a known security flaw, and bigger models weren't any safer at it. So the thing that got scarce wasn't the ability to produce code, it's the ability to look at a pile of AI-generated code and know which 45% to be suspicious of.
I think a lot of people are still building their resume around "I can prompt an LLM to build an API endpoint" when the actual hire-able skill is "I can tell you why that endpoint's auth check is wrong before it ships." Those are very different muscles and only one of them is getting more valuable.
Feels like the junior-to-senior gap used to be about speed and experience. Now it's shifting to be about judgment specifically — catching what a fast, confident, wrong answer looks like.
what's the skill you've noticed becoming more valuable now that everyone can generate a first draft in seconds?

author: Unknown Author
text:
Your plant doesn't need more AI hype. 

Every boardroom is saying "do something with AI."
 
But only a few plants managers know what to do.

Suppliers pitch AI solutions that promise transformation but rarely deliver it. Meanwhile, plant engineers are expected to integrate these systems into environments with zero tolerance for failure, with almost no grounding in how any of it actually works.

Five things every Industrial plant manager should know:

1. AI ≠ ML. And ML ≠ ChatGPT.

AI is the goal. 
ML is one method to get there. 
LLMs are one narrow branch of ML, trained on text. In industrial plants, ML mostly looks nothing like ChatGPT, it looks like supervised models predicting free lime, unsupervised models finding kiln operating regimes, reinforcement learning tuning fuel setpoints in real time.

Next time someone says "AI," ask: which type of ML, and why is it right for this problem?

2. The model is not the product. Your data is.

No architecture survives bad data. 
Pyroprocess environments are brutal, sensors drift, analysers run cleaning cycles, thermocouples lie. Before any model sees your data, it has to be cleaned, filtered, and validated. Continuously. Not once.

Ask suppliers: how often do you retune the model, and is it automatic? Then ask if your own data is accessible, connected, and recorded, 6 months minimum of consistent history is the floor, not the ceiling.

3. A model that performs well in training means nothing.

What matters is the test set, data the model has never seen. That's your only real proxy for production behavior. Overfit models look brilliant on paper and fall apart on the plant floor.

4. Complexity is not a badge of honor. Explainability is the win condition.

Linear regression, random forests, neural networks, each has a place. But in an environment with zero tolerance for failure, a model that can't explain its own recommendation is a liability, not an asset. Techniques like SHAP exist precisely so you can ask "why" and get a real answer,  not a black box.

5. This isn't future technology. It's already running.

Soft sensors predicting free lime every 15 minutes instead of waiting 2 hours for a lab result. Digital twins simulating setpoint changes before you act. Optimisers closing the loop entirely, testing every adjustment against your objective function and setting the plant automatically.

The technology is mature. The application gap is what's holding adoption back.

If you are a plant engineer reading this, you don't need to become a machine learning engineer. You need enough grounding to ask the right questions, spot the red flags, and defend the decisions you make.

That's the whole point.

author: Abayomi Abiodun
text:
After an AI conference, I asked a hiring manager:

"When hiring an AI Engineer or Data Scientist, what's the first thing you look for?"

I expected to hear Python, Machine Learning, or LLMs.

Instead, he said:
"I want someone who can solve a business problem, not someone who only knows how to build a model."

That answer has stayed with me.
Many aspiring AI professionals spend months chasing the latest frameworks, while employers are asking a different question:

Can this person create value for our business?
Imagine two candidates.

Candidate A has an impressive tech stack, Python, TensorFlow, LangChain, Docker, Azure, and more, but struggles to explain the business impact of their projects.

Candidate B has solid technical skills but demonstrates how they built an AI assistant that reduced response times, integrated with existing systems, improved user satisfaction, and increased operational efficiency.

Who gets the offer?
In industries like healthcare, employers need more than AI expertise. They need professionals who can understand workflows, integrate with existing systems, protect privacy, collaborate across teams, and measure real outcomes.

The skills that stand out:
- Strong AI fundamentals (ML, LLMs, RAG, AI Agents, evaluation)
- Software engineering and deployment
- Data preparation and analysis
- Cloud and production experience
- Communication and collaboration
- Business thinking
-  Responsible AI practices

Throughout my experience mentoring aspiring AI professionals, working on enterprise AI projects, and speaking with recruiters, one pattern keeps emerging:
The people who stand out aren't the ones with the longest list of AI tools on their CVs.
They're the ones who connect technology to business value, collaborate effectively, and build solutions that solve real problems.

Frameworks will evolve. New models will emerge.
But the ability to solve meaningful problems, communicate effectively, and keep learning will always be in demand.
Because companies don't hire AI professionals simply for knowing the latest framework.
They hire them to deliver results.

If you were hiring for an AI role today, what would matter most: technical depth, business understanding, communication skills, or the ability to combine all three?

author: Madhuvanthi Ravi
text:
The H-1B just got a $100,000 price tag. And nobody in my network is talking about the number that matters more... GCC hiring in India grew 3.4x since 2021.

From the time I was in college, the smartest people I knew had one playbook.  Crack a US offer, get the visa, build the career abroad. That was "making it."

That playbook just got a lot more expensive. And meanwhile, the centers that used to be called "back offices" are now where P&L ownership sits, where AI products get built end to end, where 4-10 year experienced folks are commanding comp that didn't exist five years ago.

64% of new GCC roles this year need AI or data skills. AI engineers are seeing 18-25% salary inflation. Annually. Tier-2 cities aren't the fallback anymore - they're the strategy.

Here's the part I won't skip past, because skipping it is how you lose credibility on this topic.

The same GCCs are also laying people off. Intel ran a second round through its Bengaluru and Hyderabad centres this year. Salesforce's "AI-first" reorg touched its India delivery teams too. This isn't a one-way boom.

But look at where the cuts are landing versus where the hiring is happening. The cuts are hitting 6-10 year mid-tier folks doing maintenance and legacy delivery work. The hiring is in AI/ML platform, data engineering, security. Same building, two completely different job markets.

So "GCCs are safe" was never the real claim. The real claim is narrower: if your skillset is the one AI tooling is replacing, no geography saves you right now - not Bengaluru, not Boston. And if your skillset is the one GCCs are actively short on, both geographies are paying you more than they were three years ago.

I'm not saying leaving India is the wrong call. It was never a wrong call. I'm jsut saying.. that the old binary - leave for growth, stay for stability - doesn't hold anymore. The real fault line runs through your skillset, not your passport.

If you're 27 and weighing an offer letter right now - the flight and the visa stamp aren't the variable that decides your next five years anymore. Your skillset is. That's a much harder, much better problem to solve.

text:
Most people will focus on the robot. 🤖

The more important story is what sits behind it.

Google DeepMind’s Gemini Robotics 2 shows how quickly the gap between AI reasoning and physical action is beginning to close. A humanoid robot that can walk, crouch, manipulate objects and complete multi-step tasks is impressive, but the real development is the model’s ability to understand its environment, plan ahead and coordinate its whole body through one connected system.

For years, AI has performed best in digital environments, while robotics has relied on separate systems for perception, movement and decision-making. Gemini Robotics 2 points towards a future where those capabilities are brought together.

That changes the conversation for employers.

The key question is no longer whether robots will become more capable. It is how organisations will redesign work when AI can reason, respond and act in the physical world. 🧠

That will create demand for people who can work across robotics, machine learning, computer vision and physical AI, while also understanding how these systems fit into real operating environments.

The organisations preparing their workforce and talent strategy now will be better placed to turn embodied intelligence into practical value.

author: Hamsa Medhat, open to work
text:
I'm excited to share that I have achieved an A+ on my Bachelor's Thesis at the German University in Cairo! 🎉
Over the past several months, I developed an Explainable Resume Matching System Using Natural Language Processing (NLP), designed to make AI-powered recruitment more accurate, transparent, and trustworthy.
The system follows a two-phase pipeline. First, it parses resumes and job descriptions, performs exact and semantic skill matching using a fine-tuned E5 embedding model, and applies a LightGBM classifier to determine whether a candidate is qualified for the role. Qualified candidates then move to the second phase, where they are ranked using configurable weighted criteria such as skills, experience, education, certifications, and an optional cross-encoder reranker. Finally, the system generates human-readable explanations for every decision using a Large Language Model, allowing recruiters to understand why a candidate was selected or rejected instead of relying on a black-box prediction.
In addition to intelligent resume matching and ranking, the system includes:
1-Resume and job description parsing.
2-Explainable AI for transparent hiring decisions.
3-Comparative candidate analysis.
4-Automated interview scheduling through Google Calendar integration and email notifications.
5-A recruiter-friendly web application that streamlines the recruitment process.

I'm proud that the proposed system achieved 96.00% accuracy, 92.86% precision, 92.86% recall, and a 92.86% F1-score, outperforming several state-of-the-art approaches while addressing one of the biggest challenges in AI recruitment systems: explainability.
This project has been an incredible learning journey that strengthened my knowledge in Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing, Machine Learning, Explainable AI, Information Retrieval, and full-stack software development. More importantly, it taught me how to transform research into a practical system that solves a real-world problem.
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to Associate Professor
Milad Ghantous, PhD for his continuous guidance, invaluable feedback, and unwavering support throughout the implementation of this project. Your mentorship played a significant role in helping me achieve the best possible outcome.
Finally, I would like to thank my family, friends, and everyone who supported and encouraged me throughout this journey.
I'm excited for what comes next and look forward to building AI systems that create real impact.

author: Unknown Author
text:
The biggest forecasting problem in European SMEs isn't the wrong model — it's no model at all.

Most small and mid-sized businesses still rely on manual projections built from last quarter's numbers and intuition. That approach breaks the moment demand shifts, a supplier delays, or a seasonal pattern deviates. Time series forecasting exists to replace that fragility with structure.

The landscape of available methods has expanded dramatically. Classical statistical approaches like ARIMA handle stable, linear patterns well. But real business data — with its irregular seasonality, external shocks, and compounding variables — increasingly demands machine learning and AI-driven models that adapt to complexity without hand-tuned parameters.

Here's what gets overlooked: the sophistication of the model matters far less than the quality of the data pipeline feeding it. Inconsistent historical records, missing data points, and poorly defined variables will sabotage any forecast, no matter how advanced the algorithm. Data readiness is the actual bottleneck.

SMEs that treat forecasting as core operational infrastructure — not a finance-team side project — make faster, sharper decisions on inventory, cash flow, and hiring.

What excites me most is the emphasis on solving real-world challenges—not just publishing research, but translating cutting-edge AI into production systems that power the next generation of collaborative and autonomous robots. The role also encourages collaboration across engineering teams and contributions to leading research venues such as CoRL, ICRA, NeurIPS, and CVPR.

author: Apurva Parad
text:
A year ago, I left Amazon for a startup. I had no idea where it would take me.

At a company like Amazon, the machine runs itself. Processes exist for everything. Someone, somewhere, has already solved the problem you're facing. You focus on your slice, and the rest hums along in the background.
At Whistlemind, there is no background hum. There's just me, my team, and every part of the business like sales, delivery, hiring, cash flow & client relationships. All landing on my desk, often on the same day. The hardest part wasn't the big decisions. It was the small ones that never stop. Getting real visibility into what's actually happening across the business & not what a dashboard says, but what's really going on. That takes constant, deliberate effort when you don't have layers of people doing it for you.

And somewhere in the middle of learning all this, I had to learn something else: how to keep myself standing. I said yes to the business and, too often, no to myself. A year in, I'm still learning. But I'm not the same person who walked in on day one and I'm grateful for every hard week that got me here.

To every woman building something of her own, juggling a business, a body, a family, and a hundred quiet expectations no one talks about. I see you. This one's for us.

author: Mark Healy
text:
Bridging the Gap Between University and Industry.

This is where many engineering graduates get stuck.

Not because they didn't work hard at university.

But because nobody showed them how to transition into industry.

Not because they didn't work hard at university

Industry expects engineering value.

They're not the same thing.

At university you learn subjects like:
• Fluid Mechanics
• Thermodynamics
• Structural Analysis
• Finite Element Analysis
• Electrical Machines
• AutoCAD
• SolidWorks
• MATLAB
Every one of those subjects has value.

But employers aren't hiring graduates simply because they completed those subjects.

They're hiring graduates who understand how engineering businesses actually operate.

Can you explain how a consulting engineer estimates work?

Do you understand the difference between a client, consultant, contractor and equipment vendor?

Do you know how projects move from concept through fabrication, installation and commissioning?

Can you confidently discuss the industry you're applying to?

That's the gap.

And it's much bigger than most graduates realise.

Over the past 13 years, I've seen graduates spend months—and sometimes years—sending online applications with little success.

Then, once they begin learning how their chosen industry actually works, everything changes.

Their confidence improves.

Their conversations become more meaningful.

Managers start taking them seriously.

Interviews become easier because they're speaking the language of the industry.

Whether you're interested in Mining, Energy, Building Services, Water, Food Manufacturing or Infrastructure...

The goal isn't simply to finish your degree.

The goal is to become someone an engineering manager can confidently picture working in their business.

That's the gap you need to bridge.

Because degrees get you to the starting line.

Industry knowledge gets you across the finish line.

text:
🎓 GSEPプログラムで「AI in Modern Industry」をテーマに講義を行いました！
Recursiveの Yago del Valle-Inclan Redondo と Matthew Whalley が、GSEPプログラムの学生の皆さまに向けて、「AI in Modern Industry」をテーマとした講義を行いました。✨

講義では、AI、機械学習、Large Language Models（LLM）の基礎から、環境・産業分野におけるRecursiveの実際のAI活用事例までをご紹介しました。

Yagoは、気象データのダウンスケーリング、地下水位予測、水道管の漏水検知など、ScienceAIの取り組みを紹介しました。AIと物理モデル、観測データを組み合わせ、複雑な環境課題に取り組むアプローチを共有しました。
Mattは、ニューラルネットワークとLLMの仕組み、さらにAIエージェントやマルチエージェントシステムについて解説しました。技術的な基礎から、実際のビジネス・産業への応用までをつなぐ内容となりました。
多様な専門分野を学ぶ学生の皆さまからは、環境科学、AIの品質、研究への応用に関する質問が寄せられ、講義後には研究連携やインターンシップの可能性についても意見交換を行いました。🤝

またRecursiveは、先日OpenAI Partner NetworkにおいてOpenAI Advanced Partnerに認定されました。日本で掲載されている5社のうちの1社として、企業におけるAI活用を実践的な成果へとつなげるプロジェクトに取り組んでいます。

📈 Recursiveでは、AIを活用して環境・産業の課題に取り組む技術職・ビジネス職のメンバーを募集しています。採用情報とOpenAI Advanced Partnerに関する投稿は、コメント欄のリンクからぜひご覧ください。⬇️

[English]
🎓 Sharing “AI in Modern Industry” with the GSEP Program
Recursive’s Yago del Valle-Inclan Redondo and Matthew Whalley recently delivered a lecture for students in the GSEP Program under the theme “AI in Modern Industry.” ✨

The session covered foundational concepts in AI, machine learning, and large language models, alongside real-world examples of how Recursive applies AI to environmental and industrial challenges.

Yago introduced Recursive’s ScienceAI work, including weather downscaling, groundwater-level prediction, and water leak detection. These examples demonstrated how AI can be combined with physics-based modeling and observational data to address complex environmental challenges.

Matt then explored how neural networks and LLMs work, as well as AI agents and multi-agent systems. The session connected technical foundations with practical applications across business and industry.
Students from diverse academic backgrounds raised thoughtful questions on environmental science, AI quality, and research applications. Following the lecture, we also exchanged ideas with students and faculty about potential research collaboration and internship opportunities. 🤝

As one of five OpenAI Advanced Partner Network companies listed in Japan, we are excited to continue delivering practical AI projects that help organizations turn AI opportunities into real-world outcomes.

author: Unknown Author
text:
🚨 A candidate can ace the interview... and still fail the job within a few weeks.
More often than not, it isn't the candidate.
It's who was sitting on the other side of the table.
Take a Data Engineering or Machine Learning role.
The interviewer is often the engineering manager who happened to have bandwidth that week.
They're excellent at shipping backend services.
But they may have never:
• Built or versioned a feature store.
• Debugged model drift in production.
• Evaluated what "good" looks like for a Data team at a Series B company versus a Series D company.
So the interview naturally shifts toward what the interviewer knows.
➡️ Generic problem-solving.
➡️ Syntax questions.
➡️ Whiteboard exercises borrowed from an entirely different discipline.
The interview ends up measuring:
"Can this person code?"
Instead of:
"Can this person succeed in this role, this domain, and this stage of the company?"
The consequences don't show up during the interview.
They show up months later.
❌ False Positives — Great interview performance, poor execution on the job.
❌ False Negatives — Strong specialists rejected because they didn't fit the interview format.
❌ Re-interviewing — Teams quietly repeating interview rounds because nobody fully trusts the first evaluation.
❌ Mis-hires — The most expensive hiring mistake, yet rarely traced back to where it actually began.
The further a role moves away from a company's core engineering expertise, the harder it becomes for internal interviewers to accurately assess it.
That's not a people problem. It's a structural one.
A technical hiring bar is only as strong as the person holding it.
For Data, AI, and Product roles, that person should have lived the role—not just know how to read the code.

author: Sanskar A.
text:
Most candidates spend hours adding 30–50 skills to their resume.

But here's what many recruiters actually do first:

They scroll straight to the Projects section.

Why?

Because skills tell us what you claim to know.
Projects show us what you've actually done.

Imagine these two candidates:

Candidate A
Skills: Python, SQL, Power BI, Machine Learning, Excel, AWS...

Candidate B
Project: Built a sales dashboard using Power BI that analyzed 50,000+ records, reduced reporting time by 40%, and automated weekly reports using SQL.

Who leaves a stronger impression?

The second candidate.

A well-written project section answers the questions recruiters care about:
✅ What problem did you solve?
✅ Which tools did you actually use?
✅ What was your contribution?
✅ What measurable impact did you create?

Instead of listing every technology you've ever touched, focus on 2–5 meaningful projects.

A simple formula works well:

Problem → Your Action → Tools Used → Result

This approach makes your resume easier to trust and much easier to remember during short resume screenings.

Recruiters don't hire skills on paper.
They hire people who can apply those skills to solve real business problems.

How do you write your project section today—just a title, or does it tell a complete story?

text:
4) Agentic AI: The Next Evolution

Today, we are witnessing another important milestone in Artificial Intelligence.

This new phase is called Agentic AI.

While Generative AI primarily responds to prompts, Agentic AI goes several steps further.

An AI agent can:

- Understand a goal.
- Break it into smaller tasks.
- Make decisions.
- Use tools.
- Gather information.
- Adapt when circumstances change.
- Continue working toward completing the objective.

Imagine hiring an intelligent assistant.

Instead of asking,

"Write this email."

You say,

"Organize my business trip to Berlin next month."

An advanced AI agent could potentially:

- Search for suitable flights.
- Compare hotel options.
- Create a travel itinerary.
- Schedule meetings.
- Prepare travel documents.
- Monitor changes.
- Notify you if adjustments become necessary.

Rather than performing one isolated task, Agentic AI coordinates multiple tasks to achieve a broader objective.

This shift moves AI from being an assistant that answers questions to becoming a collaborator that can help execute complex workflows.


Why This Evolution Matters

Every stage of AI has solved increasingly sophisticated problems.

• Machine Learning helped computers learn from data.

• Deep Learning enabled computers to recognize highly complex patterns.

• Generative AI empowered computers to create new content.

• Agentic AI is enabling systems to plan, coordinate, and complete increasingly complex tasks with greater autonomy.

👉 This progression is transforming industries around the world.

👉 Healthcare is becoming more data-driven.

👉 Financial institutions are improving fraud detection.

👉 Manufacturing is becoming more automated.

👉 Education is becoming more personalized.

👉 Agriculture is becoming more precise.

👉 Scientific research is accelerating.

👉 Businesses are improving customer experiences while automating repetitive work.

The opportunities are enormous, but so are the responsibilities.

As AI systems become more capable, organizations and governments must also address important questions about privacy, transparency, accountability, fairness, security, and responsible use.

Innovation and responsibility must progress together.

author: Yogesh Kumar, open to work
text:
1111 Days Ago, I Started With Just One Problem. Today, I'm Looking for One Opportunity. 🚀

Three years ago, I made a simple decision that completely changed the way I approached learning. I promised myself that no matter how busy life became, I would solve at least one coding problem every single day. There were days when I had classes, internship deadlines, office work, and countless moments when I felt too tired to continue. Many times I wanted to skip a day, telling myself that missing just once wouldn't matter. But I kept coming back, one problem at a time.

Today, that small promise has turned into a 1111-day LeetCode streak.
Looking back, I realize this journey was never about maintaining a streak or collecting badges. It was about building discipline, sharpening my problem-solving skills, and developing the habit of learning every single day. Every challenge taught me to think more clearly, write better code, and approach complex problems with patience instead of frustration.

That mindset didn't stay limited to coding platforms. It became the foundation of everything else I built. It helped me work on AI applications, backend systems, full-stack projects, and solve real engineering problems. More importantly, it taught me that growth comes from consistency, not from occasional bursts of motivation.

Now, I'm ready for the next chapter of my journey.

I'm actively looking for opportunities as a Software Engineer, Backend Engineer, AI Engineer, Machine Learning Engineer, or Full Stack Developer. I'm excited to join a team where I can keep learning, solve challenging engineering problems, and contribute to building products that create real impact.

If you're hiring, or if someone in your network is looking for an engineer who genuinely enjoys solving problems and continuously improving, I'd truly appreciate an opportunity to connect.

Sometimes all it takes is one conversation to change a career. Maybe this post reaches the right person.

Thank you to everyone who has supported me along the way. Here's to the next challenge, the next lesson, and hopefully, the next opportunity. 🚀

熟悉 Python、SQL、統計分析或預測模型，喜歡從資料中找出問題原因，並將分析結果應用在實際場景。

熟悉 Linux、Network、Storage、Cloud、Container、GPU 或大型系統環境其中一項，並對系統穩定性與效能優化有興趣。
【Software／Application Engineering】
具 Python、Backend、API、Database 或系統整合經驗，喜歡處理實際產品與複雜應用問題。
【DevOps】
熟悉 CI/CD、Linux、Automation、Deployment 或 Release Flow，希望參與更完整的軟體交付流程。
【Quality Assurance】
具軟體測試或測試自動化經驗，熟悉 API、System Testing、Integration Testing 或 Python 者尤佳。
【Frontend Engineering】
熟悉 React、TypeScript 或現代前端開發，對資料呈現、系統操作介面與使用者體驗有興趣。

author: Lamees Butt
text:
Last week it was our PM Andy Burnham quietly championing RISER™. This week VIDEO HIRING was making the headlines and RISER featured in the The Times and Sunday Times! 📰 

Mad to think that some of the first reactions I got when I founded the company was "Video? Really???"

Every conversation was a pitch, a sell of the vision - what the world, the future of work will look like and thus what infrastructure it needed. 

Early adopters got it, it’s how the founding team and cap table was built, on humans who just get it. 

Having a vision for how the future will look, isn't about just having an idea. It's listening hard enough to the market, understanding the actual problem, and using data and calculated risk to bet on where the solution needs to be, before anyone else agrees with you.

That's how RISER™ came to be. And in the beginning, the immediate pushback was exactly that: video? Why not just use AI to automate the screening / interview and speed up the process everyone already knows?

Over the last year, we've watched what removing the human even further from this process does... 

A wave of bots, agent automation and AI wrappers that sound sexy in a demo but have eroded the trust it took decades to build and guess what, didnt actually solve the real problem.

It's been getting harder to ignore that the market has quietly turned to video anyway, with startups like SULT™ executing their hiring with video, Milly G. & Henry Porpora essentially casting for their next hire rather than filtering for one and entrepreneurs like Simon Squibb rejecting the CV in favour of wanting to see what more the individual could offer. 

Why does that matter?

Because this isnt just noise, its signal the market is ready to move away from keyword qualification, skills listed on a page, and toward casting the right person for a role based on their behaviour, their character, and how they actually show up. It’s why RISER is built on the bedrock of our proprietary technology, a machine learning algorithm that surfaces exactly that. Human to human connection based on the right fit. Giving you that 'Verified Gut Feel™'. 

Add the political agenda now backing this shift, and the momentum is impossible to miss. We are so here for it.

Thank you Olivia and the The Times and Sunday Times for featuring RISER™ and Suz this week. 🚀

RISER™. Stand out. Get matched.

author: Yechan Mun
text:
Machine Learning Specialization — Stanford Online and DeepLearning.AI. Three courses, finished this week.

I did not take this to add a line to my profile. I took it because of a decision I keep making, and I wanted to know whether I was making it for the right reason.

In every product I have shipped, I deliberately did not use a model where you might expect one. Risk detection in a children's counselling tool runs on a 33-term rule dictionary, not an LLM, and the code says "the judgment is human." A credentialing system used in hiring runs on a rule-based narrative engine with a source field on every sentence, so any line traces back to the exact input. I chose rules over learning both times.

Until now I could defend those choices on principle. What I could not do was say precisely what I was giving up.

Now I can. I understand what a decision boundary is and why a linear one fails where a neural network does not. I understand why an anomaly detector is the right shape for a rare-event problem and a classifier is not. Which means the counselling case was the correct call — the labelled data does not exist, and a false negative there is not a metric, it is a child — and the credentialing case was correct for a different reason: it is not that a model could not do it, it is that nobody should be rejected by a system that cannot show its reasoning.

Same decision. Two different reasons. I could not have written that sentence a month ago.

The point of learning where a model does work is knowing, honestly, where you chose not to use one.

author: Frankline Makarios’ profile
text:
One of the quietest shifts in business this year isn't happening in technology. It's happening in hiring.

As AI takes over more routine work, many organizations are reducing entry-level positions while increasing demand for experienced professionals who can exercise judgment, challenge assumptions, and make decisions under uncertainty. At the same time, finance leaders are reporting that AI is changing workflows faster than it is changing organizational capability.
Most discussions frame this as a workforce problem.

I think it's a leadership problem.

For decades, businesses relied on junior roles to build tomorrow's managers. Those positions weren't just about productivity; they were where people learned context, developed commercial instinct, and made mistakes with manageable consequences.
If those learning environments disappear, the real shortage won't be AI skills.
It will be decision-makers.

The organizations that outperform over the next decade won't simply automate faster. They'll redesign how expertise is transferred, how judgment is cultivated, and how future leaders are developed in an age where machines can complete tasks but cannot accumulate wisdom.

Technology can accelerate execution.
It cannot compress experience.

text:
Investors, ROI, and the Environment.
An entrepreneur friend of mine texted me today with a video of 🌈 Borys Musielak (an early-stage startup investor) talking about his investment in Shen AI - a medical deep-tech startup that essentially measures blood pressure from a smartphone face scan.

He said he decided to invest only because he knew the founder personally and because the founder already had a prior exit (even though it was in an entirely different industry - gaming). Without that personal connection, he would have passed.
He mentioned that it was tough at the beginning - lots of research, hard to build client trust, etc. - but once they entered the market, their revenue went from 0 to $200k in year one, and jumped from $200k to $2M the following year.

When I see things like this, to be completely honest, I’m not even sure what I feel...
On one hand, it validates everything I think about DeepTech and HealthTech - it's brutal to break into, but once you're in, it’s practically impossible to displace 😅
On the other hand - they got funded at the idea stage, on pure concept. They had the backing and support to make it happen. Connections and the right ecosystem are simply everything.
Meanwhile, I have to reach that exact same milestone - credibility, validation studies, and market entry - completely on my own, without any safety net or funding. Working at my dad's vegetable stall just to pay for tokens, recruiting a team on pure vision and technical documentation with zero payroll budget, and being forced to learn how to code and build the entire system single-handedly once I realized that without an MVP, no one would give me a single cent... 😑

Life isn't fair. But then again, nobody ever promised it would be, so no surprises there.

On the flip side, I'm realizing I don't even need the grace of investors right now 😅 I recruited an exceptional team that is already advising and helping me, I mastered coding and built far more than just a basic MVP - and if you don't believe me, just go to hyperion-performance.app and open DevTools (more than one Stanford CS student would envy what I built completely on my own without a CS background in Replit in just two months 😉). On top of that, a professor offered me a PhD track, I'm currently writing our first scientific paper, and I've mapped out a full validation roadmap under the affiliation of the Wrocław University of Health and Sport Sciences - which, by the way, doesn't cost me a single cent 😅 
So I guess I'm not doing too bad. 

Where others need a check for a few hundred thousand dollars just to get started, I deliver through pure determination and raw execution 😎
My ROI is going to be astronomical in a few years 😂

author: Richard Ronayne
text:
Why Is It So Difficult to Find Compliance Professionals in the Data Centre Industry?
The data centre sector continues to grow at an unprecedented pace, driven by cloud adoption, AI, digital transformation, and increasing regulatory scrutiny. Yet one challenge remains consistently overlooked:
Finding experienced compliance professionals.
While organisations compete fiercely for engineers, project managers, and operational talent, the shortage of compliance specialists is becoming equally critical.
Why?
✅ The skillset is highly specialised.
A strong compliance professional needs far more than a knowledge of regulations. They must understand operational risk, information security, data privacy, critical infrastructure, audit requirements, customer expectations, and increasingly, environmental and sustainability obligations.
✅ Industry experience matters.
Compliance in a data centre is very different from compliance in financial services, healthcare, or manufacturing. Understanding uptime requirements, resilience standards, customer audits, ISO frameworks, and operational controls takes years to develop.
✅ Regulatory complexity is increasing.
From GDPR and cyber security requirements to environmental reporting and emerging regulations governing critical infrastructure, the compliance landscape continues to evolve. Organisations need professionals who can navigate complexity while enabling business growth.
✅ The role requires a unique balance.
The best compliance leaders are not simply policy writers or auditors. They must be able to influence stakeholders, challenge decisions when necessary, and work collaboratively with operations, engineering, security, legal, and commercial teams.
✅ Demand is outpacing supply.
As more data centres are built globally, the pool of experienced compliance professionals is not growing at the same pace. Companies are often recruiting from the same limited talent market, making competition intense.
The reality is that compliance is no longer a back-office function. It has become a strategic capability that underpins customer trust, operational resilience, and business growth.
For data centre operators looking to strengthen their compliance programmes, attracting and retaining the right talent may be one of the biggest challenges they face over the next decade.

⭐️ Star Employee Awards⭐️

Just over a year ago, we were expanding both our Mobile Patrol Team and our 24/7 Control Room. Rather than recruiting solely from within the security industry, we made a conscious decision to look for people with the right character, work ethic and desire to learn.

We recruited 3 young men with no experience and trained them the Copeland way!🙌🏻📈

⭐ Ayatt Safiyullah
Whilst carrying out routine patrols and lock and unlock duties, Ayatt noticed a gentleman who appeared confused and distressed. Rather than simply driving past, he stopped to check on his welfare.
Realising something wasn't right, Ayatt contacted the police and remained with the gentleman until officers arrived.
Police later confirmed the gentleman had been reported missing three days earlier, was more than 20 miles from home, and was suffering from mental health issues.
Ayatt wasn't required to stop. He wasn't required to get involved. But he did.
Because sometimes being a security professional means being a decent human being first. His actions may well have prevented a tragic outcome.

⭐ George Lynch
George responded to a confirmed intruder activation at one of our prestigious motor dealership clients in Liverpool.
Our TrakNet AI platform detected three individuals attempting to gain access to vehicles on the forecourt, immediately alerting our 24/7 Control Room.
Controllers dispatched George while simultaneously requesting police attendance.
Within minutes George was on site, confronting and containing the suspects long enough for Merseyside Police to arrive and make arrests.
His calm, decisive actions prevented what could have been significant criminal damage and theft, protecting both our client and their assets.

⭐ Charlie Devitt
Charlie was the Control Room operator on duty during the same incident.
Using the skills he has developed over the past year, Charlie quickly identified the suspects on our CCTV system and continuously tracked their movements around the site. Throughout the incident he kept George fully updated, coordinated the police response and ensured everyone involved had an accurate picture of what was happening.
Even after George arrived on site, Charlie remained focused on the cameras, monitoring George's safety, watching for any further offenders or aggressive behaviour and recording every key event within our Digital Daily Occurrence Book.
His calm, professional approach ensured both George and the attending police officers knew exactly what they were walking into.

This incident perfectly demonstrated that successful security isn't just about the officer on the ground—it's about the teamwork between our Mobile Patrol Drivers and our 24/7 Control Room. Charlie's professionalism behind the screens was every bit as important as George's actions on the ground.
These three young men are proof that experience can be taught, but attitude, integrity, compassion and professionalism cannot!

Congratulations guys!👏🏻👏🏻

author: Brett Lewis’ profile
text:
Do hiring managers rely too heavily on virtual job interviews when recruiting?

Since becoming Prime Minister two weeks ago, Andy Burnham has criticised employers' reliance on virtual interviews when recruiting staff. While video interviews have become a standard part of the hiring process since COVID and offer clear benefits for employers and candidates, they also have limitations that should not be overlooked.

Advantages
1) Faster hiring process – Interviews can be arranged quickly without travel or room bookings
2) Lower costs – Reduces travel expenses and time away from work for both parties.
3) Greater flexibility – Easier to coordinate interviews across different locations and time zones
4) Wider talent pool – Enables employers to interview candidates from anywhere in the UK or internationally.
5) Improved scheduling – Managers can fit interviews around busy diaries more easily.
Quicker screening – Ideal for first-stage interviews before inviting shortlisted candidates in person.
6) Easy recording – Interviewers can review responses or share them with colleagues.
7) Environmentally friendly – Eliminates unnecessary travel, reducing carbon emissions.

Disadvantages
1) Limited personal connection – Building rapport is often harder through a screen
2) Technology issues – Poor internet, audio or video problems can disrupt interviews
3) Reduced ability to read body language – Non-verbal communication is less visible.
4) Candidate disadvantage – Some strong candidates are less comfortable on camera and may under perform.
5) Environmental distractions – Background noise or interruptions can affect professionalism.
6) Less accurate assessment of cultural fit – It's more difficult to judge how someone will interact with a team.
7) Risk of outside assistance – Candidates may receive prompts or use AI tools during remote interviews

As a recruiter, I believe virtual interviews should remain part of the hiring process, especially in the early stages. However, candidates should meet the hiring manager in person and visit the workplace before accepting an offer. Face-to-face interviews provide a better assessment of personality, body language and cultural fit, while allowing candidates to experience the working environment and make a more informed decision.

What are your views on this?

author: Chris Brown
text:
If it's not already happening, then don't be surprised when People teams become the practical owners of AI literacy at work - even where Legal, IT or Security formally owns AI compliance.

This matters because the EU AI Act is no longer something companies can place entirely on the "someday later" list.

Some requirements have already applied, others are still to come:
- Prohibited AI practices and AI literacy obligations have applied since February 2025.
- Obligations for general-purpose AI models began applying in August 2025.
- Further provisions, including certain transparency requirements, became applicable yesterday.
- High-risk AI rules covering areas such as recruitment, employment and worker management are currently scheduled (let's see if this actually sticks) to apply from 2 December 2027.

Early-stage companies already have a never-ending to-do list. They don't need to build an enterprise level AI governance programme.

They do need some operating basics:
- A record of the AI tools being used across recruiting and People processes.
- Defined rules on what employee and candidate data may be entered.
- Human accountability for hiring, performance and pay decisions.
- Role-specific AI literacy for employees using these tools.
- A basic review before anyone connects the latest shiny US product to the ATS or HRIS.

For founders and People leaders, now is a good time to establish these basics - before AI usage becomes too messy.

author: Brano Vargic
text:
BOB DYLAN: The times they are a-changin.....

A CEO showed me an recruitment agency quote last week. Three weeks to launch. A few thousand up front. Personas, a video shoot, a monthly retainer. The full legacy package.

We ran the same roles in 48 hours. Two hundred dollars. Three candidates by day one. He is about to become a paying customer.

Old world, meet new one.

That got me thinking about legacies. Who clings, and why. The loudest offender wasn't recruiting. It was venture capital.

I raise money, so I collect the questions. Let me translate a few from legacy into 2026.

"Are you full time? Fully dedicated?"
Me? No. Not the way you mean. But my teammates Ignacio, Roberto, and Mauro are, 24/7. Does that count?  They are also AI agents.

"Is your CTO a shareholder?"
 My CTO is AI. The day I can vest equity in a digital identity, you will be the first to know. Until then, I ship the product myself.

"How big is the team?"
 Small on purpose. The leverage isn't headcount anymore, and my burn proves it.

"Come back when you have more conviction."
 Conviction is not a diagnosis. It is a feeling in a lab coat.

Before anyone files this under bitter-founder-venting: it isn't. This is a wave, already in motion. 
Spend an hour in r/startups or r/venturecapital and you read the same story on repeat. 

Revenue and a path to profit reads as "lack of ambition." 
Capital efficiency looks "suspicious." 
Solo founder is a "red flag." 

Even insiders are writing that venture needs new filters, and the business press calls pattern matching the industry's favorite tool and its biggest blind spot.

Here is the "fuzzy" part, said without heat. Most of them are not being dumb. They are being middlemen. The money isn't theirs. It answers to LPs sitting one more legacy behind, so the safe answer has to travel up the chain. 

The checklist is risk aversion wearing a suit. And the same model that passes on a profitable founder will fund a story with no product.

That is the tell. Kodak knew about digital. Nokia saw the iPhone. Knowing was never the problem. Letting go was.

The market already moved. Revenue-first, lean, AI-native looks wrong on the old checklist, and it is exactly what wins now. The "safe" bet became the risky one.

I am not bitter. I am building through it. Revenue up, break-even in sight. When you don't need the table, you stop playing by house rules.

So, a real question, not rhetorical: what legacy is your industry defending, right up until the day it can't?

author: Andre Ordonio, SPHR
text:
Unpopular opinion: Workday Recruiting is the most expensive “free” product in enterprise software.

After 20+ years implementing Workday HCM (dating back to R12), I’ve reached a hard line: I no longer take Workday Recruiting implementation projects. I’d still recommend a best-of-breed ATS like Lever or Greenhouse every single time.

Here is why companies fall into the trap:

• The CFO/IT View: “We already own Workday HCM. Why pay for another ATS?” On paper, consolidation means lower licensing costs and fewer integrations.

• The Reality: Recruiter efficiency drops, hiring managers get frustrated, candidates face friction (great talent op to skip), and Ops spends months trying to recreate basic workflows. Meanwhile, your talent team is blocked from leveraging modern AI matching and automation tools that actually speed up hiring.

This also creates friction across HRIS/IT and their customers (the People function) because of the poor tooling and lost productivity.

The “free” ATS quickly becomes a massive hidden cost through lost productivity and slower time-to-hire.

The core issue? Enterprise standardization and recruiter optimization are not the same objective.

Too many companies select enterprise software based on executive reference calls, sales decks, or bundled convenience; while the people who live in the system eight + hours a day get zero say.

How to fix it: Run a structured software bake-off!!!

Instead of buying a bundled name, put candidates through a rigorous evaluation:
1️⃣ Give every vendor the same real-world scenarios.
2️⃣ Involve the actual practitioners; recruiters, coordinators, Ops, HRIS, and hiring managers.
3️⃣ Score objectively on workflow flexibility, candidate experience, reporting, and true Total Cost of Ownership.
4️⃣ Talk to companies that left the platform, not just the vendor's references.

As a candidate, when I click "Apply" and see a Workday URL, my expectations drop instantly. Fair or not, it signals an organization where Talent Acquisition was forced to inherit enterprise software rather than choose the platform best suited for hiring.

Technology should enable the business; not force the business to adapt to the tech.

Curious to hear from TA and HRIS leaders:

Have you been through a true software bake-off? 

Did your final selection align with the highest-scoring solution, or did executive consolidation win out? 👇

author: Shimron Equiano
text:
Years ago, before Jonothan Bosworth, I worked for a D2C sales company. One of the tactics I used to grow my team was to go to the job centre and ask if I could put a table in the corner of the room and invite people to be interviewed, to join my team.

The staff looked at me as if I'd 'grown another head', but they let me do it all the same... I did end up recruiting people this way!  It was clunky & unorthodox, but it was a start!

---

Fast forward 15+ years, as an experienced technology recruiter, I was able to generate close to 1M in annual contract-revenue/turnover, from my desk alone.

(No, I don't have any of that money left, so I cannot invest in your A.I. start-up, sorry 😅 )

---

I'm able to draw a line back to that summer, in the job centre, as a 21 year old, and I recognise that even back then I wasn't scared of hard work, being uncomfortable, or understanding that 'reps now' meant 'results later'.

Oh, and that 1M in contract-revenue/turnover was actually 3 years in the making, because '3 years prior', I called the company's Director of IT at least fifteen times without an answer! 

Every time I called, his PA fobbed me off.

He eventually emailed me, to suggest a time to speak.

When I finally got him on the phone, all he said was: 

"Can you get here tomorrow morning?"

I didn't check my diary, I didn't check my bank, I just said:

"Yes"

After a 3 hour train & tube journey, I'm sat in front of the person I'd spent weeks and months trying to get on the phone.

▪️He was direct.
▪️He was a bit abrupt.
▪️He was borderline, rude.

But I was able to look past this, because I saw the 'bigger picture'.

What happened next, was crazy 🤯

A couple of weeks later, I was on the way to collect my daughter from school, and my mobile phone rang...  

..It was a candidate who wanted to apply for the role given to me by the Director of IT in this story...

The only problem. This candidate had no 'sector' experience, but he talked a good game, and he convinced me to do all that I could to secure him an interview.

✅I got him the interview.
✅He got the job.
✅We were both happy.

And here's the twist...

Shortly after, the Director of IT was fired and an interim CIO joined the organisation to take his place. The CIO asked all the staff 'who the best suppliers were'

My candidate (the one with no 'sector' experience) called me to give me a 'heads up'. He said:

"Shim, there's a new sheriff in town, I've put in a good word for you. He's going to give you a call, as he's planning a big talent acquisition drive. Be ready"

- - -

I've never been so 'anxious' for a phone call!! ☎️

Long story short:

1. The call went well.
2. The presentation that followed went well.
3. The service delivery thereafter went well.

1M gross sales later, the moral of the story is this:

The uncomfortable, hard work you do today, may not show up in your results, until many years from now, so just do the work, without 'checking your abs in the mirror' every day.

author: Gregory Turkawka
text:
The EU AI Act date everyone was watching was Sunday.

Most of the coverage said it moved. Half of that is true. The high risk obligations for hiring systems, the risk assessments and the bias testing and the human oversight and the registration in an EU database, slid to December 2027. Sixteen extra months, and a lot of teams read that as permission to stop thinking about it.

The transparency duties under Article 50 did not slide. They took effect on 2 August, on the original schedule, and the power to fine for breaking them arrived on the same day.

So the disclosure obligation is not a 2027 problem. It was live yesterday. If a system talks to a candidate and does not tell them they are talking to an AI, that gap is open now.

I wrote about this two weeks ago, before the date landed, inside a longer argument. An AI recruiting agent you can ship in a weekend is standing on three things it does not own: someone else's burn rate, someone else's export policy and a model's willingness to invent the fact it is missing. This summer all three moved.

The part I keep coming back to is that the answer is not more automation. It is less of it, set down more carefully. Decide with plain logic whatever plain logic can decide, and only reach for the model when the logic genuinely cannot settle it. Route across providers so no single one can take you offline. And never let the model originate a claim about a person.

That last one is the whole thing for me. The record belongs to the person it describes, and it has to be true before the model ever looks at it.

A system built that way is explainable because it was always explainable, not because someone retrofitted it in 2027.

Essay in the first comment.

author: Joseph Sack
text:
Somewhere right now a guidance counselor from 2004 is having a very bad day.

The CEO of Randstad, the largest staffing company on planet Earth, just told CNBC that "the days of going to college and doing something in an office, they are over." This is a man with nearly 5,000 offices in 39 countries whose entire job is knowing where the jobs are. He is not a guy in a Lambo yelling at a phone camera. He is the actual adult in the room, and the adult in the room just flipped the table.

Let's sit with the irony for a second. The institution that spent decades selling us "get a degree, get a cubicle, get a pension" is now getting disrupted by a chatbot that never went to prom, never took the SATs, and definitely never did a keg stand at a mixer to network its way into an internship. AI skipped the entire four year experience and went straight to doing the job. Rude, honestly.

Meanwhile the plumber your parents told you not to become is out here clearing six figures and laughing at all of us who spent four years and a small mortgage learning to write emails that a language model now does for free in .8 seconds.

Here's the part that is less funny and more "oh no." That whole college to cubicle pipeline was never really about what you learned. It was a stamp. A permission slip. Proof you sat still long enough and paid the toll booth on the way to being hired. AI does not care about your stamp. It cannot be impressed by your GPA. It just wants to know if the work gets done, and increasingly it can do a lot of that work itself, minus the coffee breaks and the group projects where one person does everything.

Data centers still need concrete poured and conduit run though. Turns out the robots need a building to live in, and buildings do not build themselves no matter how good your prompt is. So skilled trades wages are up 30 percent since 2022 while a lot of entry level office roles are getting quietly replaced by software that never calls in sick.

I did not wait around to find out which side of this I'd land on. I built the tech stack for two companies with AI tools and zero dev team, because the old gatekept way needed capital and credentials I did not have. Turns out I did not need them either. The gate just wasn't as locked as everyone said it was.

So here is the actual paradigm shift, minus the doom and gloom. It was never trades versus tech versus college. It is gatekept paths versus self built ones. The people in trouble are not the ones without a diploma. They are the ones who never learned to build or prove anything without someone else's permission slip first.

Somewhere a career fair booth is being quietly repurposed into an AI trainer recruiting table as we speak.

Curious where you land. Overdue reality check or overhyped headline?

Most boards think their biggest constraint is technology.

It isn’t. 

It’s leadership capability.

Two years of boardroom attention has gone into AI, geopolitical risk and supply chains. Capital is flowing. Tools are more accessible than ever. And yet the organisations pulling ahead aren’t the ones with the best technology - they’re the ones with leaders who know how to redesign work, reallocate decision-making between humans and AI, and execute through ambiguity.

Harvard Business Review’s 2025 Prize-winning research put it plainly: competitive advantage won’t come from adopting AI. It will come from how leaders deploy it.

That reframes the real board-level question. 
Not “have we invested enough in technology?” but:

👉 Do we have the leadership bench to actually use what we’ve bought?

👉 Are we recruiting for today’s org chart, or the one we’ll need in three years?

author: Roxy Green
text:
The most valuable thing I’ve built over the last 15 years isn’t my network, my reputation, or my results. It’s trust.

Behind every ‘Open to Work’ conversation is a human being trying to make a decision that could completely change their life. 

Perhaps they’re searching for a better future, more money, more time with their children, a chance to finally feel valued, a chance to leave a toxic environment, or a chance to become who they know they’re capable of being.

Maybe that’s why the relationships I’ve built have lasted. Over the years, I’ve had people come back to me again and again throughout their careers, not because I convinced them to take jobs, but because I treated them like people first. 

Sometimes that meant telling someone not to take a role, having difficult conversations nobody else wanted to have, or supporting someone through rejection, burnout, redundancy, self-doubt, or complete career uncertainty. 

The reality is that people rarely remember the recruiter who sent the most LinkedIn messages; they remember the one who made them feel seen.

Recently, I reread a recommendation that described me as becoming part of someone’s ‘personal board of directors’ throughout their career. That comment alone means more to me than any placement, target, or title ever could. 

Recruitment done properly leaves a mark far beyond the hiring process. Years later, people still recommend me to friends, introduce me to leadership teams, ask for advice before making career moves and come back because trust was built long before there was ever an opportunity on the table. That kind of trust cannot be automated, faked, or built through transactional recruiting.

This industry talks endlessly about AI, speed, output and productivity, yet the recruiters who will still matter five years from now are the ones who understand something technology never will. People are not CVs, careers are not pipelines, and human connection will always outperform process.

To everyone who has trusted me with their career, their fears, their ambitions, their next step, or even just an honest conversation over the years, thank you. You’ve reminded me that the most important part of this job was never placing people; it was making sure they never felt alone while navigating change. 

Careers change, companies change, markets change, but people never forget how you made them feel. 

❤️

5. Why The First Ten Hires Matter

Building a Future-Products Lab - 5/18  

The first ten hires become the lab's operating system.

They decide the culture before any leader writes it down. They decide how disagreement feels, how ambitious the work becomes, how much craft is expected, and how the team speaks to the wider company.

At Apple, the AI/ML incubator lab grew from nothing to a team of ten. I cared about disciplinary strength, but I cared just as much about fit, overlap and emotional weather.

Early hires should not duplicate each other too heavily. The first group needs broad coverage: someone who can shape a system, someone who can test an assumption, someone who can make a prototype real, someone who can argue from the user, someone who can visualise the future in a way stakeholders understand.

Skill overlap becomes useful later. At the start, too much overlap creates blind spots.

Culture also travels outward. If the first team presents a confused story, the lab becomes easy to dismiss. If they speak with one clear voice, the organisation starts to understand what the lab is for.

The first ten people are not headcount. They are the first proof of the lab's judgement.

author: MD DANISH
text:
HR just stopped being "support" and became strategy.

Not next year. Now.

AI disruption. Global pay transparency lawsuits. Talent markets that don't play by one region's rules anymore.
HR didn't ask for a seat at the table. It got pulled into one — with no warning and no manual.
Here are 5 shifts every leader needs on their radar in 2026:
1. Agentic AI is already here
 This isn't chatbots scheduling interviews anymore. AI is making context-aware decisions inside your workforce, right now.
 The danger isn't how fast it's spreading. It's that governance isn't spreading with it.
2. Degrees are losing. Skills are winning.
 Skills-based hiring is the fastest-growing shift in HR — and for good reason. It's more portable. More equitable. It works across borders with wildly different credentialing systems.
 The smartest companies aren't just hiring for skills. They're building internal talent marketplaces — so expertise moves within the company instead of walking out the door.
3. The "one HR leader does everything" era is over
 AI governance. Hybrid culture. Employee experience. Compliance.
 That's not one job anymore. It's four.
 Companies operating across multiple markets need fundamentally different HR structures than single-region businesses. Copy-paste HR doesn't scale globally.
4. Pay transparency isn't a policy. It's legal exposure.
 Courts are now applying state pay laws across borders using "sufficient nexus" — meaning pay equity isn't a regional HR task anymore. It's a company-wide compliance risk.
 Pay Equity Ratio shouldn't live in an annual audit. It belongs on a live scorecard, tracked like revenue.
5. HR is cutting HR
 Recruiting. D&I. L&D.
 These teams are getting cut — while simultaneously managing every other department's layoffs.
 That's not a budget story. That's a warning sign that HR capacity needs the same planning rigor as any other business-critical function.
The pattern underneath all five:
 HR is no longer reacting to the business. It's architecting it — AI governance, talent mobility, pay defense, organizational capacity.
The leaders who treat this as strategy now will set the standard.
 The ones who wait will be managing the fallout instead.
Which of these five is hitting your organization hardest right now?

author: Probal Rudra
text:
🤖 AI in HR: Don’t Start With the Technology. Start With the Work.

The biggest mistake organisations make with AI in HR?

They ask: “Where can we use AI?”

A better question is:

“Which HR work should no longer be done the way we do it today?”

AI adoption in HR is not about adding another tool to the HR tech stack. It is about fundamentally redesigning how work gets done.

Here are 7 practical tricks to accelerate AI adoption in HR:

1️⃣ Start with pain points, not AI
Identify repetitive, high-volume, low-value activities across Hire-to-Retire — then ask where AI can remove friction.

2️⃣ Automate the “moments that matter”
Recruiting, onboarding, employee queries, career development, performance management and manager support are ideal starting points.

3️⃣ Build AI into the flow of work
Don’t expect HR teams to open another application. Embed AI into the systems they already use — HRMS, ServiceNow, Teams, email and employee portals.

4️⃣ Move from Chatbots → Copilots → Agents
The evolution is important:
💬 Answer questions
🤝 Assist HR professionals
⚙️ Execute processes

The real transformation begins when AI agents can safely orchestrate multi-step HR processes.

5️⃣ Treat data as the foundation
AI + poor HR data = faster bad decisions.

Invest in:
• Data quality
• Process standardisation
• Governance
• Skills & job architecture
• Integration

6️⃣ Put humans in the loop
AI should augment HR judgement — not blindly replace it.

Especially for decisions involving:
⚖️ Employee relations
💰 Compensation
📈 Performance
👥 Talent
🔐 Personal data

7️⃣ Measure business impact — not AI usage
Don’t celebrate “10,000 AI queries.”

Measure:
📉 Cost per transaction
⏱️ Cycle-time reduction
📈 Employee experience
🎯 HR productivity
💰 Cost avoided
🚀 Business value created

The HR AI maturity curve

Digitise → Automate → Augment → Predict → Act

The future HR organisation won’t simply have an AI strategy.

It will have AI embedded into the operating model.

And perhaps the biggest mindset shift:

AI won’t replace HR professionals.
HR professionals who know how to work with AI will increasingly outperform those who don’t.

The question for CHROs is no longer:

“Should we adopt AI?”

It’s:

“Where do we redesign HR work first?”

author: Lisa H., open to work
text:
Last night at 7.19pm I had a response to a job ad I’d applied for. 20 minutes later I was invited to interview. Brilliant I thought! I’ve made an impression here. Let’s go! Then I dug into the email and my heart sank. 

It’s one of those AI video interviews with an assessment. You have to respond in a specific format within a set or limited retakes. 

Only once you’ve managed to navigate this madness and once again have the AI decide if you did well enough do you get put forward for ‘review’ by the hiring team. 

Note that the email claims, with some jubilation, that the next interviews (plural) will be live videos.

I don’t know whether to laugh or cry (probably the latter to be honest as it’s bill payment day) but needless to say I have removed myself from applying. 

This is not how we should be recruiting. For many people, especially more mature candidates, introverts or neurodiverse candidates this kind of thing is just terrifying and will not show us at our best. It disadvantages certain groups. 

We do better with face to face conversations talking about our skills with a real person and bouncing the conversation back and forth. This AI method is cold, unwelcoming, impersonal and devoid of personality. 

It feels like a cake was dangled under my nose only to be taken away. 

Companies, please stop doing this and just have proper conversations with real people. 

Yours, a scared job seeker looking for someone to give her a break.

author: Fanny Püschel
text:
66 Prozent der Jugendlichen wollen einen Beruf, in dem sie etwas herstellen. Nur 24 Prozent halten das Handwerk für hochtechnologisch.

Diese Lücke ist dein Recruiting-Problem. Und du schließt sie, ohne eine einzige Stellenanzeige zu schalten.

Die Zahlen stammen aus dem AI Jobs Report 2026 von Autodesk. Befragt wurden 1.000 Schülerinnen, Schüler und Studierende zwischen 14 und 23 Jahren sowie 500 Fachkräfte, allerdings in den USA. Der Wunsch, etwas mit den Händen zu schaffen, liegt dort sechs Prozent höher als 2024. Bei der Frage, welche Arbeit im KI-Zeitalter attraktiver wirkt, entscheiden sich die Jüngeren mit mehr als zwei zu eins für die physische statt die digitale Welt.

Gleichzeitig verbinden 60 Prozent Bau, Fertigung und Handwerk vor allem mit manuellen Fähigkeiten. Nur 24 Prozent beschreiben diese Bereiche als hochtechnologisch.

Der Nachwuchs will also genau das, was du anbietest. Er weiß nur nicht, dass in vielen Betrieben längst Aufmaß-App, digitale Zeiterfassung und CAD zum Alltag gehören.

Jetzt der Teil, den die meisten übersehen: Wo informiert sich diese Generation? 80 Prozent wollen sich berufsrelevante Fähigkeiten über YouTube-Videos aneignen. Weniger als jede fünfte Person nutzt dafür ein Praktikum. Das Bild von deinem Beruf entsteht am Bildschirm, lange bevor jemand deine Werkstatt von innen sieht.

Dazu kommt: 82 Prozent dieser Altersgruppe fühlen sich im Umgang mit Claude, Gemini und ChatGPT sicher. Fragt ein 17-Jähriger dort, ob Anlagenmechaniker ein zukunftsfähiger Beruf ist, baut die Antwort auf Texten auf, die irgendjemand geschrieben hat. Schreibt kein Betrieb auf, wie digital die Arbeit wirklich ist, bleibt die Antwort beim Klischee. Sichtbarkeit in der KI-Suche ist hier kein Bonus obendrauf. Es ist derselbe Text, der auch deine Karriereseite trägt.

Was du dafür dokumentieren kannst, in normalen Sätzen auf deiner eigenen Website:

Welche Software auf der Baustelle läuft und was sie dem Team abnimmt.
Wo ihr KI schon einsetzt, bei Angeboten, Aufmaß oder Dokumentation.
Wie ein echtes Projekt abläuft, von der Planung bis zur Übergabe.
Wie die Einarbeitung aussieht und wer sich in den ersten Wochen kümmert.

Das ist kein Employer-Branding-Projekt. Das sind vier Seiten Text, die Fragen beantworten, die sonst niemand beantwortet.

Wie viel dabei auf dem Spiel steht, zeigt eine Stepstone-Analyse: Junge Akademiker in Deutschland brauchen im Schnitt 40 Bewerbungen für ein Vorstellungsgespräch, mit Berufsausbildung sind es 26. Die Ausbildung ist gerade der stabilere Weg. Nur erfährt das kaum jemand von den Betrieben selbst.

Mach den Test: Frag ChatGPT oder Perplexity, ob dein Ausbildungsberuf zukunftsfähig ist. Taucht in der Antwort irgendein Betrieb aus deiner Region auf? Schreib gern in die Kommentare, was du bekommst.

author: Alexandra Wudel
text:
Ein Gesetzestext allein schützt niemanden. 

Er braucht Regeln, wie man ihn tatsächlich umsetzt. Genau die bekommt der EU AI Act jetzt zum ersten Mal 🙌🏾 

🌟 KI-Gesetz-Expert*innen sprechen von einem Meilenstein im Gesetzgebungsprozess und das sehe ich genauso!

Kurz zur Einordnung, falls dir "harmonisierter Standard" bisher nichts sagt: 

1️⃣ Der AI Act schreibt vor, was Hochrisiko-KI-Systeme leisten müssen, etwa beim Qualitäts- oder Risikomanagement. 

2️⃣ Wie Unternehmen das konkret umsetzen, steht dort nicht. Genau diese Lücke füllen harmonisierte Standards, technische Vorgaben der europäischen Normungsorganisationen CEN, CENELEC und ETSI. 

3️⃣ Wird ein Standard im EU-Amtsblatt zitiert, gilt für Unternehmen, die ihn anwenden, eine Konformitätsvermutung. Sie müssen dann nicht mehr im Detail beweisen, dass sie das Gesetz einhalten.

Und genau das ist jetzt zum ersten Mal passiert im Kontext des EU AI Acts ⤵️

🔹 EN 18286 hat den Normungsprozess komplett durchlaufen ▶️ Der Standard zum Qualitätsmanagementsystem für Hochrisiko-KI-Systeme (Artikel 17 AI Act) wurde am 12. Juli 2026 von CEN-CENELEC final verabschiedet, als erster von allen Standards im gesamten JTC-21-Arbeitsprogramm. Zuständig ist das Gremium JTC21 unter der Leitung von Sebastian Hallensleben 🇪🇺 (Chair), Patrick BEZOMBES (Vice-Chair) und Kim Skov Hilding (Secretary).

🔹 Ein großer Schritt, aber noch nicht die volle Rechtswirkung ▶️ Damit sich Unternehmen wirklich auf die Konformitätsvermutung verlassen können, muss der Standard noch im EU-Amtsblatt zitiert werden. Das ist der letzte Schritt, der aktuell noch aussteht. Drei weitere zentrale Standards, unter anderem zu Cybersicherheit und KI-Vertrauenswürdigkeit, befinden sich inzwischen ebenfalls in der öffentlichen Konsultation, die bis Ende 2026 fertiggestellt sein soll.

⚖️ Für alle in KI-Governance, Compliance oder Produktentwicklung ist das der Moment, an dem ein abstrakter Gesetzestext zu einer konkreten, anwendbaren Prozessvorgabe wird. 

👥 Für wen ist das gerade besonders relevant?

▶️ Anbieter von Hochrisiko-KI-Systemen (z. B. in Recruiting, Kreditvergabe, Bildung, kritischer Infrastruktur): Ihr bekommt zum ersten Mal eine konkrete Vorlage dafür, wie ein QMS nach Art. 17 auditierbar aussehen muss, statt eigene Interpretationen des Gesetzestexts zu riskieren.

▶️ Compliance und QM-Verantwortliche: Wer schon mit ISO 9001, ISO 13485 oder ISO/IEC 42001 arbeitet, kann jetzt konkret prüfen, wo die eigenen Prozesse anschlussfähig sind und wo Lücken bleiben.

▶️ Notified Bodies und Auditor*innen: Für sie entsteht damit erstmals ein gemeinsamer Prüfmaßstab, was Bewertungen konsistenter und planbarer macht.

▶️ Policy- und Regulatory-Teams: Wer die Entwicklung der übrigen Standards (Cybersicherheit, Vertrauenswürdigkeit, Bias) im Blick behalten will, sieht an EN 18286, wie der Prozess von der Konsultation bis zur Verabschiedung konkret abläuft.

author: Dr. Guido Norman Motz
text:
Seit Sonntag ist die KI-Verordnung komplett anwendbar. Der Teil, der Recruiting und Zeitarbeit am meisten trifft, wurde 6 Tage vorher verschoben. 
 
Der 2. August 2026 galt lange als der große Stichtag des EU AI Act (Verordnung (EU) 2024/1689): Ab diesem Tag sollten die strengen Pflichten für Hochrisiko-KI greifen. Dazu zählt ausdrücklich KI im Beschäftigungskontext: Bewerberauswahl, Einstellungsentscheidungen, Aufgabenzuweisung, Leistungs- und Verhaltensüberwachung (Anhang III Nr. 4 KI-VO).
 
Daraus wird vorerst nichts. Mit der Digital-Omnibus-Verordnung (EU) 2026/1744, in Kraft seit dem 27. Juli 2026, hat die EU diese Pflichten auf den 2. Dezember 2027 verschoben. Was bedeutet das konkret für Personaldienstleister, Personalvermittler und Recruiting-Teams?
 
1. Was seit Sonntag gilt: Die Transparenzpflichten des Art. 50 KI-VO. Recruiting-Chatbots müssen sich als KI zu erkennen geben. Bei KI-Texten ist die Pflicht enger: Sie entfällt im Fall einer menschlichen Prüfung mit damit verbundener redaktioneller Verantwortung (Art. 50 Abs. 4 UAbs. 2 KI-VO). Verstöße sind bußgeldbewehrt. Deutschland hat die Aufsicht scharf geschaltet: Seit dem 29. Juli ist das KI-MIG in Kraft. Die Bundesnetzagentur ist zentrale Marktüberwachungs- und Beschwerdestelle.
 
2. Was schon länger gilt: Die Verbote des Art. 5 KI-VO, darunter das Verbot der Emotionserkennung am Arbeitsplatz und auch im Bewerbungsgespräch per Video-Analyse. Die Pflicht zur KI-Kompetenz des Personals wurde durch den Omnibus dagegen zur bloßen Förderpflicht abgeschwächt.
 
3. Was auf Dezember 2027 verschoben wurde: Das volle Hochrisiko-Programm für KI in der Personalarbeit. Wer Matching-Software, CV-Parser oder KI-gestützte Einsatzdisposition etc. nutzt, wird hierdurch Betreiber eines Hochrisiko-Systems, verbunden mit Pflichten zu menschlicher Aufsicht, Schulung und Information der Beschäftigten und des Betriebsrats vor deren Inbetriebnahme (Art. 26 KI-VO).
 
4. Die offene Flanke der Branche bleibt: Setzt der Kunde KI ein, um überlassene ZAN auszuwählen, einzuplanen oder zu bewerten, wer ist dann Betreiber und wen treffen die Informationspflichten? Wird der Kunde angreifbar oder gerät der PDL in die Schusslinie? Für das Dreiecksverhältnis der AÜ gibt die Verordnung darauf keine ausdrückliche Antwort. Genau diese Frage sollten PDL und Kunden bis Ende 2027 vertraglich klären.
 
Für Disponenten und HR heißt das praktisch: Jetzt ist Zeit zu erfassen, welche KI in den eigenen Recruiting- und Dispositionsprozessen steckt, also von der Stellenanzeige, dem Targeting bis zum Matching-Tool. Anschließend sind die verbliebenen 16 Monate als Umsetzungsfenster zu nutzen und nicht als Pause zu verstehen.
