🔍 Excited to share a project I built: HireSignal — a transparent, auditable candidate-screening dashboard designed around one core principle: fairness auditing over black-box ranking.
Most "AI hiring" tools hide their logic. HireSignal does the opposite:
✅ Fully transparent, weighted scoring model — every weight visible and adjustable, no hidden ML decisioning on the ranking itself ✅ Built-in fairness audit using a four-fifths-rule-style check across proxy groups (never actual protected-class data — only role-relevant fields + separate synthetic proxy labels used solely for auditing) ✅ Plotly visualizations flagging any group whose pass-through rate falls notably below average — surfaced for human review, never an automated block ✅ Offline, rule-based qualifications summarizer that strictly reports job-relevant skills/experience/achievements and is explicitly designed to never reference or infer age, gender, race, ethnicity, disability, or other protected characteristics ✅ Full compliance-ready audit log export (CSV/Markdown) — every score, every component, every threshold, timestamped
Built with Python + Streamlit, runs 100% offline/open-source (no API keys, no paid cloud services) — deployable directly to Streamlit Community Cloud or Hugging Face Spaces.
The goal isn't to automate hiring decisions — it's to give recruiters and TA teams a tool that makes scoring logic and fairness gaps visible, so humans stay firmly in the loop.
"This tool supports human recruiter judgment and fairness review; it does not make final hiring decisions."

Hollywood Fights AI In Public While Quietly Building It Into Movies: 

Even as Hollywood performers protest and Hollywood studios sue "in their war on AI," reports the Los Angeles Times, "the entertainment industry is deepening its dependence on it."

Among hundreds of job postings in late June, more than one in 10 was likely connected to AI. The top studios' public postings suggest they have been recruiting people to build AI tools. They are also recruiting teams to defend their intellectual property against unauthorized AI use. "There are plenty of studios that are hiring [for AI] but never talk about it in public," said Yoland Yan, a co-founder of ComfyUI, a company that helps studios juggle different AI tools. Companies have been hesitant to detail how they use generative AI in film production — partly because they are concerned about consumer and union backlash. Some in Hollywood described AI use as the new cosmetic surgery, where everyone knows it is happening, but few will admit to it...

Although some companies may be shy about sharing their AI plans, big stars who don't have to answer to others have been more open about their embrace of the new technology for storytelling. Rejecting AI is like picking a horse and buggy over a car, said "Star Wars" creator George Lucas. "Artificial intelligence means it's much easier for us to make movies," he told a trade magazine earlier this year. "There's nothing you can do about it. That's progress. It's the future." Some in Hollywood have a softer stance on artificial intelligence, with studios cutting deals with AI companies, and filmmakers like Martin Scorsese backing AI companies. Ben Affleck launched an AI film tech company then sold it to Netflix for half a billion dollars. When launching InterPositive, Affleck said he wanted to keep "storytelling human" by building AI tools that could fix lighting, generate missing shots and other things while "keeping creative decisions in the hands of artists...."

Disney, Netflix and Amazon had job postings that were about using AI on the creative side of the business. Universal, Paramount, Warner Bros. and Sony had job ads suggesting they were also using AI but for marketing, distribution and audience analytics. text:
𝗔𝘀𝗸 𝗮 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀: 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀.

Almost every hiring team we talk to has bought some AI in the last year. When we ask what it actually does, the honest answer, more often than not, is scheduling.

That’s not a criticism. It’s just what the data shows too. The 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗿𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 report found that scheduling automation is the single most widely scaled AI category in recruiting, and even then it only reaches meaningful requisition coverage at about a third of companies. So the most common form of “AI in hiring” right now is a tool that finds a time on a calendar. Useful, but it’s the shallowest end of the funnel.

Here’s what we keep coming back to. Scheduling is the easiest thing to automate because it doesn’t ask for any judgment. Nobody worries about whether the calendar tool was fair. The hard, valuable parts of hiring, the sourcing, the screening, the ongoing conversation with a candidate, the internal coordination to actually close, those need judgment, and that’s exactly why most tools stop short of them.

What we’ve tried to build is the opposite of that. Four agents that run the actual funnel and hand off to each other. Sourcing finds and reaches out. The interview agent screens on technical and behavioural depth. The engagement agent keeps candidates warm on WhatsApp and email. The ops agent handles the internal back-and-forth. Which means the work moves end to end without a recruiter stitching each step together by hand.

And the point of all that is not to remove the human. It’s the reverse. When the agents carry the transactional load, the recruiter spends their time where judgment actually matters, calibrating with the hiring manager, reading a shortlist properly, making the call. The decisions stay human. The admin doesn’t.

That’s the difference between having AI in your process and having AI run your process. One saves a few minutes on scheduling. The other changes what your team spends its week on.

author: Jennifer Chimamaka Okafor
text:
Some Mondays, the hardest part isn't the work. It's not knowing if anyone will ever understand why you're doing it.

In 1901, divers pulled a corroded lump of bronze out of a Greek shipwreck. For over 50 years, nobody understood what they were looking at. 
It sat in a museum drawer, misfiled as scrap.

It wasn't scrap. It was a machine built by Greek engineers around 100 BCE, a hand-cranked device with interlocking gears precise enough to predict eclipses and track the sun, moon, and planets. 

Something that sophisticated wouldn't be built again for over a thousand years.

Whoever engineered it did work so far ahead of their time that their own world had no place to put it. 

It took modern X-ray imaging, decades later, for anyone to finally understand what they'd actually built.

I think about that every time I do the unglamorous, unseen part of the work, the research nobody's asked for yet, the reading, the slow thing with no audience. 

It's tempting to think unseen means unimportant. 

The people who built the Antikythera mechanism died without ever knowing the world would eventually understand them. 

Their work was real before anyone recognized it.

If today feels like you're building something nobody around you understands yet, that's not a sign to stop. 

That may be exactly what it feels like right before it's understood.

What are you building right now that hasn't been recognized yet? 

Tell me. I want to hear it, today of all days.

New here? I am Jennifer Chimamaka Okafor, UN & Global Health Strategist, an MPH candidate bridging AI, ML, Epidemiology, and Public Health across Africa and globally. UNICEF · WHO · BudgIT Foundation. Follow for daily evidence-based insights.

author: Kristy Natasha Y., open to work
text:
One year ago, I was building machine learning systems for fraud detection and customer-service AI.

Over the last three months, I've been applying many of the same machine learning principles to a completely different problem: predicting asteroid tidal-disruption outcomes from SPH simulations for my MSc research at Imperial College London.

The objective isn't to replace physics simulations. Instead, it's to quickly identify which scenarios can be screened with a machine learning surrogate and which still require computationally expensive SPH simulations running on Imperial's High Performance Computing (HPC) cluster.

Some highlights from the project:
• Trained on 489 SPH simulations (218 GB of data) generated on Imperial's HPC cluster
• Developed physics-informed features to improve generalisation
• Used group-aware cross-validation to prevent simulation leakage
• Achieved a grouped held-out R² of 0.923
• Built an interactive trust-aware dashboard to help scientists understand when the surrogate can be relied upon

Looking back, I've had the opportunity to work on machine learning across three very different domains:
• Fraud detection in fintech
• AI systems for telecommunications
• Computational planetary science

Different industries, but the same challenge: turning complex, messy data into reliable decisions.

I'll be completing my MSc this September and am looking for ML Engineer, Applied Scientist, or Data Scientist opportunities starting in October.

A few months ago, I wrote my first line of code for a Machine Learning algorithm.
Today, I looked back at that project.
It was Linear Regression on the California Housing dataset, and what started as a simple regression model slowly turned into one of the biggest learning experiences in my AI/ML journey.
I learned that building a model is much more than calling .fit().
Here's what I explored throughout the project:
•Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
•Data visualization (heatmaps, scatter plots, geographical maps)
•Train-test split & feature scaling
•Linear Regression from scratch
•Cross-validation & model evaluation
•Ridge & Lasso Regularization
•Hyperparameter tuning with GridSearchCV
•Comparing models instead of relying on a single metric

Looking back, I can see mistakes in that notebook—and I'm actually happy about that.
Every notebook is a snapshot of what you knew at that moment. This one reminds me that progress in Machine Learning doesn't happen overnight. It comes from experimenting, making mistakes, asking questions, and continuously improving.
This project may not be my most advanced one anymore, but it will always be special because it was the one that taught me how to think like a machine learning engineer.
"What was the first ML project that changed how you think about data?"
On to the next algorithm. 🚀

author: Lucky Solomon
text:
Seven weeks ago I started posting consistently about AI and Africa.

I want to share what has happened since — not to impress anyone, but because I think it challenges something a lot of African professionals believe about LinkedIn.

The belief: LinkedIn only works if you already have a big name, a prestigious title, or thousands of followers.

What I've experienced: the opposite.

In seven weeks of posting three times a week, I have had conversations initiated with researchers from Ethiopia, founders building Nigerian language AI products, professors connected to Harvard working on ML education for the Global South, and early-career engineers looking for direction in Embedded AI.

None of these people knew me before I started posting.

Every single connection came because I showed up consistently, wrote about something I genuinely cared about, and said something specific enough to be useful.

Here is what I think is actually happening:

LinkedIn's global AI conversation is loud. But it is also very homogeneous — dominated by voices from the US, UK, and a handful of Asian tech hubs. When an African voice enters that conversation with a specific, well-reasoned perspective, it stands out immediately. Not because it is louder. Because it is different.

The African perspective on AI is not just a cultural addition to the global conversation. It is a technical corrective. We understand constraints that Silicon Valley does not have to think about. We understand what it means to build for environments where the infrastructure assumptions collapse.

That perspective has value. Global value.

But only if we share it.

Seven weeks in. The experiment continues. I will keep showing up.

If you are an African researcher, student, or professional sitting on knowledge and waiting until you feel "ready" — I want you to know: the room is already waiting for you.

Start posting. Your voice belongs in this conversation.

Core adversarial machine learning theory and attack taxonomies

Domain-specific risks in computer vision, natural language processing (NLP), healthcare AI, finance, and autonomous systems

Emerging threats, privacy risks, and regulatory and legal considerations
